# Experience / Project Deep-Dive Round

[← Airbnb](../README.md) · [Every Airbnb question](../../airbnb.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/experience-project-deep-dive)

`deep-dive` `impact` `leadership` `technical-deep-dive`

---

## Requirements

- Before the interview, the candidate submits 2–3 projects, each described in a paragraph, and the interviewer selects one to explore.
- The conversation examines the project's context, the candidate's own role, decisions taken, options rejected, measurable results, and changes they would make in hindsight.
- A brief resume bullet can still trigger an extensive examination, so the candidate should be able to defend every project listed there.

## Notes

- The most repeated criticism from candidates who did not pass was that they had worked on a complicated project but could not tell its story concisely. Plan for a 20-minute main account followed by 25 minutes of discussion; using the entire hour on one project is viewed as weak communication.
- The size and reach of the work indicate seniority. A polished account of a three-person project lasting one quarter is still weaker than a clear explanation of a multi-quarter, ten-person program in which you owned a meaningful portion.
- The interviewer's position influences the emphasis of the questions: with an engineering manager, focus more on product and impact; with a staff engineer, emphasize technical trade-offs; with a director, highlight cross-functional influence.
- An interviewer's prior experience may be much closer to the candidate's area than anticipated, such as an iOS specialist evaluating someone from backend engineering; study the introduction carefully and adjust your framing.
- Typical follow-ups include: how did you find the underlying cause? what disagreement nearly threw the project off course? what would you alter? what result could be measured?
- Candidates are expected to bring a one-slide diagram or whiteboard drawing, and reports indicate that an architecture sketch makes a complicated system substantially easier for the interviewer to track.
- Behavioral questions are woven into the project conversation instead of appearing in a separate section; as the interviewer examines the work, they probe technical and non-technical matters, including team relationships and ownership of decisions.
- Interviewer interest differs substantially. Some come from an unrelated field and appear clearly disengaged, so make the account understandable on its own rather than depending on shared background. Others, sometimes individual contributors newly moved into management, question forcefully to test whether the project truly involved scope and leadership; prepare concise, supportable explanations of exactly what you owned.

## Preparation

- Choose three projects that collectively demonstrate technical depth, work across teams, and solving unclear problems, then draft a paragraph about each beforehand.
- Practice each project in a timed 20-minute run and remove anything nonessential. A rehearsal that exceeds the limit will take even longer in the actual interview.
- For each resume bullet, create three questions you would pose as the interviewer and practice responding to them.
- Prepare answers in advance for: "how did you analyze the root cause", "who challenged your view and how did you resolve the disagreement", "what was the numerical effect", and "what would you change".
- Review the interviewer's LinkedIn profile the day before and adjust the balance between technical detail and product impact based on it.
